chapter.name: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
chapter.blurb: Forming a pair of linear equations from a real-life situation, solving it graphically, classifying it by comparing ratios of coefficients, and solving it algebraically by substitution or elimination, including recognising when it has infinitely many solutions or none.

scope_in.item: Translate a real-life situation involving two unknown quantities into a pair of linear equations in two variables, using clearly named variables
Write a linear equation in two variables in the general (standard) form ax + by + c = 0
Find at least two solutions of a linear equation in two variables and plot them to draw its graph as a straight line
Solve a pair of linear equations graphically by finding the point where the two plotted lines intersect

Define and distinguish a consistent pair (unique solution), an inconsistent pair (no solution), and a dependent pair (infinitely many solutions), and match each to intersecting, parallel, and coincident lines respectively
Compare the ratios a1/a2, b1/b2 and c1/c2 of a pair of equations a1x+b1y+c1=0 and a2x+b2y+c2=0 to determine, without graphing, whether the pair is consistent, inconsistent or dependent
Solve a pair of linear equations by the substitution method: express one variable in terms of the other, substitute, solve, and back-substitute
Solve a pair of linear equations by the elimination method: scale the equations to equalise one variable's coefficient, add or subtract to eliminate it, solve, and back-substitute

Recognise, from a true statement with no variable (such as 18 = 18), that a pair solved by substitution or elimination has infinitely many solutions, and from a false statement (such as -4 = 0 or 0 = 9), that it has no solution

Represent and solve word problems -- on ages, costs, incomes and expenditures, fractions, and two-digit numbers and their digit-reversals -- as a pair of linear equations, by substitution or elimination

scope_out.item: The cross-multiplication method for solving a pair of linear equations
scope_out.reason: This chapter (Reprint 2026-27) teaches only the graphical, substitution and elimination methods; the Summary on p.37 lists exactly these two algebraic methods, with no cross-multiplication formula or section anywhere in the chapter's 14 pages

scope_out.item: Reducing equations involving terms like 1/x, 1/y, or 1/(x+y) to linear form by substituting a new variable such as u = 1/x
scope_out.reason: The Summary (p.37, point 5) only makes a passing general remark that some situations 'are not linear to start with'; no worked example or named method for this appears anywhere in the chapter's 14 pages

scope_out.item: Pairs of linear equations in three or more variables
scope_out.reason: Every situation and every worked example in this chapter uses exactly two unknowns

scope_out.item: Quadratic, exponential or other non-linear pairs of equations
scope_out.reason: The chapter title and every worked example restrict to linear equations only

scope_out.item: Matrix or determinant methods (e.g. Cramer's rule) for solving a linear system
scope_out.reason: Not part of this NCERT chapter or the CBSE Class 10 syllabus at this stage

scope_out.item: Solving a pair of equations whose coefficients are irrational (surd) numbers, as a distinct worked technique
scope_out.reason: The only mention is a passing aside on p.30 about graphs having 'non-integral' solution coordinates like (square root of 3, 2 times the square root of 7); no worked Example in the chapter's 14 pages solves an equation with irrational coefficients, and the one exercise item that appears to use them is not legible in the extracted text, so it is left out of the authored question set as a deliberate judgement call rather than a source-verified item

scope_out.item: Graphs of linear inequalities, or shading a region that satisfies an inequality
scope_out.reason: This chapter's graphical work is limited to plotting equations (equalities) and reading their intersection point; inequalities are not discussed anywhere in these pages

concepts.name: Forming a pair of linear equations from a word situation
concepts.description: Translating a real-life situation with two unknown quantities into two linear equations in two variables, each written in the standard form ax + by + c = 0.
concepts.idea: Give the two unknown quantities names, usually x and y, then turn each separate piece of information in the situation into one linear equation connecting them.
concepts.rule: Choose x and y for the two unknowns, write each given condition as a linear equation in x and y, and, if needed, rearrange it into the general form ax + by + c = 0.
concepts.example: Akhila's rides cost Rs 3 each and Hoopla costs Rs 4 a game; if x is the number of rides and y the number of Hoopla games, 'Hoopla played is half the rides' gives y = x/2, and 'total spend is Rs 20' gives 3x + 4y = 20.

concepts.name: Graphical method of solving a pair of linear equations
concepts.description: Drawing the two lines of a pair of linear equations from a table of solutions and reading their point of intersection as the solution of the pair.
concepts.idea: Every linear equation in two variables is a straight line; plotting both lines on the same graph and finding where they meet shows the pair's common solution directly.
concepts.rule: Find at least two solution points for each equation, plot both lines on the same axes, and read off the coordinates of the point where they cross as x and y.
concepts.example: For x + 3y = 6 and 2x - 3y = 12, plotting points such as (0, 2), (6, 0) and (0, -4), (3, -2) gives two lines that cross at (6, 0), so x = 6, y = 0 is the solution.

concepts.name: Consistent, inconsistent and dependent pairs by comparing ratios
concepts.description: Classifying a pair of linear equations a1x+b1y+c1=0 and a2x+b2y+c2=0 as consistent (unique solution), inconsistent (no solution) or dependent (infinitely many solutions) by comparing a1/a2, b1/b2 and c1/c2, and matching each case to intersecting, parallel or coincident lines.
concepts.idea: The relationship between the two lines -- crossing once, running parallel, or lying on top of each other -- is decided entirely by comparing the ratios of their coefficients, without drawing anything.
concepts.rule: If a1/a2 is not equal to b1/b2, the lines intersect and the pair is consistent with a unique solution. If a1/a2 = b1/b2 but this is not equal to c1/c2, the lines are parallel and the pair is inconsistent with no solution. If a1/a2 = b1/b2 = c1/c2, the lines are coincident and the pair is dependent (consistent) with infinitely many solutions.
concepts.example: For 2x + 3y - 9 = 0 and 4x + 6y - 18 = 0, a1/a2 = 2/4 = 1/2, b1/b2 = 3/6 = 1/2 and c1/c2 = -9/-18 = 1/2, all equal, so the lines are coincident and the pair has infinitely many solutions.

concepts.name: Substitution method
concepts.description: Solving a pair of linear equations by expressing one variable in terms of the other from one equation, substituting it into the second equation, and solving the resulting single-variable equation.
concepts.idea: If one equation tells you what one variable equals in terms of the other, you can replace that variable everywhere it appears in the second equation, turning two unknowns into one.
concepts.rule: Step 1: from either equation, write one variable in terms of the other. Step 2: substitute this into the other equation and solve the resulting equation in one variable. Step 3: substitute this value back to find the other variable.
concepts.example: For 7x - 15y = 2 and x + 2y = 3: from the second equation x = 3 - 2y; substituting gives 7(3-2y) - 15y = 2, i.e. -29y = -19, so y = 19/29, and then x = 3 - 2(19/29) = 49/29.

Solves y = 3 and finds x = 4

concepts.name: Elimination method
concepts.description: Solving a pair of linear equations by multiplying the equations to make the coefficients of one variable numerically equal, then adding or subtracting the equations to eliminate that variable.
concepts.idea: Scaling both equations so that one variable has matching coefficients lets you cancel that variable by adding or subtracting the whole equations, leaving a single equation in the other variable.
concepts.rule: Step 1: multiply the equations by suitable non-zero constants to make the coefficients of one variable numerically equal. Step 2: add or subtract the equations to eliminate that variable and solve the equation that remains. Step 3: substitute this value into either original equation to find the other variable.
concepts.example: For 9x - 4y = 2000 and 7x - 3y = 2000: multiplying by 3 and 4 gives 27x - 12y = 6000 and 28x - 12y = 8000; subtracting eliminates y, giving x = 2000, and substituting back gives y = 4000.

concepts.name: Recognising infinitely many solutions or no solution algebraically
concepts.description: During substitution or elimination, recognising that a resulting statement with no variable left that is always true means the pair has infinitely many solutions, while one that is false means the pair has no solution, and applying this alongside the chosen method to word problems, including two-digit numbers and their digit-reversals.
concepts.idea: If both equations are really the same line in disguise, every trace of the variable cancels out and leaves a true statement like 18=18; if the two lines are parallel, the variable also cancels out but leaves a false statement like -4=0.
concepts.rule: While solving by substitution or elimination, if the working reduces to a true statement containing no variable, the pair has infinitely many solutions (dependent); if it reduces to a false statement containing no variable, the pair has no solution (inconsistent); otherwise continue to solve for the unique values of x and y.
concepts.example: Solving 2x + 3y = 8 and 4x + 6y = 7 by elimination (double the first equation and subtract) gives 0 = 9, a false statement, so the pair has no solution.

Two different pairs of linear equations both reduce, during elimination, to a statement with no variable left. Pair P reduces to 0 = 0, and Pair Q reduces to 0 = 5. Explain what each result means for its pair, and explain why the SAME elimination process can lead to two completely different conclusions.
questions.a: Pair P (0=0) has infinitely many solutions, since the equations are equivalent. Pair Q (0=5) has no solution, since the lines are parallel but not coincident. Both start with proportional x,y coefficients (so the variables cancel either way), but they differ in whether the constant terms are also in that same proportion.
s: Explains 0=0 (Pair P) means infinitely many solutions because the equations are equivalent
Explains 0=5 (Pair Q) means no solution because the equations describe parallel, non-coincident lines
Explains that both start with proportional x and y coefficients, but differ in whether the constant terms are also in that same proportion
